extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and the moral/social sciences; readers learning to analyze arguments and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for analyzing arguments, identifying fallacies, and choosing appropriate methods in philosophical and moral/social inquiry. Emphasizes avoidance of equivocation, irrelevant conclusion, circular reasoning, and the empirical grounding of methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitio Principii / Begging the Question
rubrics_metrics.description: Asserting in the premises what is to be proved; e.g., saying that 'justice and wisdom must be something' when the intended meaning is not established, or assuming the impossibility of a minimum in arguing for infinite divisibility of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when a premise smuggles in the conclusion (verbal juggle). Examples: the infinite-divisibility argument that assumes impossibility of a minimum; Euler’s flawed argument about minus×minus giving plus (the premise requires proof as much as the conclusion). Note that such cases are often plausibly expressed and appeal to imagination, and may hide an underlying fallacy of another sort (ambiguous middle-term or a priori prejudice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous Middle-Term / Equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same word in different senses across premises so that an inference appears valid while the terms differ in import (e.g., 'something' meaning substance in one premise and merely an object of thought in another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for shifts in the meaning of key terms between premises and conclusion. When exposed, the fallacy often reduces to a different kind (confusion of senses); clarify senses before accepting the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori Fallacy / Natural Prejudice (argument from inconceivability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring impossibility or falsity from the incapacity of the imagination to conceive a case (the belief that whatever cannot be conceived cannot exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat intuitive incapacity as proof. Example: judging a minimum thickness impossible because imagination cannot conceive it. Distinguish apparent obviousness of a premise from its being distinct from the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular Reasoning / Reasoning in a Circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Deriving a conclusion by presupposing the standard or principle one is trying to establish; e.g., moral writers who take assumed 'natural' sentiments as their standard and then classify divergences as 'unhealthy' to preserve the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when a writer explains divergence from an assumed standard by declaring the divergence defective rather than revising the standard. Example: using an alleged universal sentiment as both datum and standard; Hobbesian social-compact accounts that deduce obligation from a supposed ancestral promise without justifying why we are bound by promises made for us.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoratio Elenchi / Irrelevant Conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting, often subtly, a different proposition for the one that requires proof; proving something that may excite the right emotions or dispositions but does not establish the original claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the proposition proven is exactly the one asserted. Whately’s examples: proving that a fraud is 'atrocious' instead of proving the accused committed it; making an audience laugh to destroy a defense; substituting the particular for the universal or vice versa. Avoid appeals that produce practical agreement without establishing the specific proposition (improper appeals to passions, proving a different-but-related claim). Examples include many attempted refutations of Malthus and the stock stick-knocking refutation of Berkeley (answering the wrong question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prove or disprove what was not asserted
rubrics_metrics.description: When rebutting an opponent, avoid disproving a claim that the opponent never made, or proving a proposition that was not the point in dispute (e.g., proving population can be dense and prosperous where that was not Malthus’s assertion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure counterexamples and collections of facts confront the doctrine as it is actually stated (including its qualifications). Beware of refutations that succeed only by shifting the target or by showing related but different facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Evidence and Theories of Method must be empirical, not a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of our rational faculty (principles of evidence and method) are learned by observing the agent at work; they should not be constructed a priori from abstract reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate methods by generalizing from successful procedures in concrete cases: 'We learn to do a thing in difficult circumstances, by attending to the manner in which we have spontaneously done the same thing in easier ones.' Avoid prescribing scientific method without reference to how truth has actually been ascertained in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize methods from simpler to more complex cases (inductive adaptation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The way of obtaining truth is often seen instinctively in simpler problems and then generalized by judicious adaptation to complex cases, especially in moral and social sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing method for difficult inquiries, adapt methods proven in simpler domains; recognize that earlier scientific achievements guide method construction. Use exemplification and concrete application rather than abstract precepts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stricter rules of induction in moral and social sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and social inquiries often require stricter rules of induction and careful adaptation of general scientific methods, because these subjects are more complex and controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether unsatisfactory results in moral/social inquiry stem from wrong method choice or poor application of appropriate methods; seek stricter inductive procedures and clearer exemplification when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous or misleading terminology (e.g., the word 'Necessity')
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms with strong associative meanings (such as 'Necessity') can mislead by importing implications (like irresistibleness) not intended in the philosophical doctrine; improper terms create confusion and practical misapprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise, less emotionally loaded language when expressing causal or philosophical claims. Explain technical meanings explicitly (e.g., philosophical Necessity as uniformity of sequence or predictability, not irresistibleness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical Necessity (criterion for claims about freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctly conceived: given the motives present to an individual and the character of that individual, the manner in which he will act might be unerringly inferred; i.e., actions are predictable if antecedent conditions and character are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating arguments about free will, examine whether claims rest on this interpretation (predictability from antecedents) or on an informal notion of irresistibleness. Distinguish between logical predictability and the felt consciousness of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish causation-as-uniform-sequence from fatalism/irresistibleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the doctrine that actions follow antecedents (uniformity and capacity of prediction) with the idea that agents are irresistibly compelled (fatalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the argument conflates invariable sequence with the notion that 'there is no use in struggling against it.' Note that causes can be counteracted; human actions are subject to competing causes, and the possibility of self-influence must be recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize self-formation: agents can help form their own character
rubrics_metrics.description: Although character is influenced by organization, education, and circumstances (often formed 'for' us), individuals can, by willing requisite means and placing themselves under new circumstances, alter their character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing moral responsibility or arguments about freedom, account for the agent’s capacity to form desires and habits that alter future conduct. Distinguish between ultimate origin of character and intermediate agency of self-formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad definition of 'motive' and the role of habit
rubrics_metrics.description: A motive is not always merely anticipation of pleasure or pain; through association actions can become desirable for their own sake, and habit can sustain actions even when pleasure is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyses of human action, include habits and desires for the action itself as legitimate motives. Avoid narrow analyses that reduce every voluntary act to immediate pleasure/pain anticipation.
